justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—1 day, 1 week, and 1 month—were all set at 438.6 because they represent the best forecasted central value for the underlying variable of interest (e.g., a stock price, metric, or event outcome). This value is likely derived from historical data, trends, or patterns that suggest the current conditions will largely persist across these timeframes. Over the shorter, 1-day horizon, fewer variables are expected to shift dramatically, so it is reasonable to assume that the variable will tend to revert to this central tendency in the absence of major disruptions. Across the longer-term horizons, such as the 1-month period, the point estimate remains the same because, on average, no specific directional bias is assumed to dominate over time, though uncertainty naturally increases.

The widening of the confidence intervals as the timeframe lengthens reflects an increase in uncertainty over time. Over one day, the range of plausible outcomes (90% confidence interval of 434.21 to 443.99) is relatively narrow because short-term fluctuations tend to be more predictable and constrained by recent trends or mean-reverting behavior. Over a week or a month, however, external factors, compounding risks, and random variability have more time to work their way into outcomes, leading to wider intervals of uncertainty. These sources of uncertainty might include macroeconomic developments, unforeseen shocks, shifts in demand or market conditions, or cumulative noise that becomes less predictable over time.

Finally, outcomes could fall outside the stated intervals due to specific risks or events that are difficult to anticipate or quantify. For example, a sudden financial crisis, geopolitical conflict, or natural disaster could have an outsized impact on the variable of interest, causing it to move well beyond the predicted range. Similarly, any unexpected news or events directly tied to the entity being modeled—such as earnings announcements, lawsuits, or regulatory changes—could introduce volatility beyond what the forecast accounts for. While the confidence intervals attempt to capture most of the plausible outcomes under normal circumstances, they may not fully encompass tail risks or extreme scenarios.
